catalog_quote: Vowels that are unmarked for pitch can be regarded as basically low-toned. The penultimate vowel, it will be observed, is the primary locus of pitch differences (and is also characterized by vowel lengthening, which we have not indicated in our transcriptions). [p. 142] ... Second, we assume that there is a rule in Digo that accents the penultimate vowel of the word. In accordance with general practice in autosegmental phonology, this accent will be indicated by a 'star' (*) over the penult vowel. Third, we assume that there is a rule of HIGH TONE DISPLACEMENT in Digo that says: draw an association line between a high tone and the starred (accented) vowel. (This rule will be refined somewhat as we proceed.) Fourth, we assume an additional rule that will somehow account for the fact that a high tone associated with the accented vowel is realized as a rising-falling sequence over the final two vowels when the post-penult consonant is not a voiced obstruent but as a level high tone when that consonant is a voiced obstruent. Fifth, we assume that if no high tone is associated with the starred vowel, that vowel is pronounced with a mid-falling pitch. [p. 148] ... the vowel of a root like /nen/ is pronounced long when in penultimate position in the phrase, Just as the vowel of a root like /heg/ in (l6); but the .vowel of /nen/ is pronounced short in other positions in the phrase. [p. 151]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Digo is not in the catalog. 4 sec. 4.4, pp. 161-176), is listed at p. 483 among the languages with 'culmination de longueur, mais non de hauteur, sur la pénultième' (via 'mijikenda'), and its Annexe profile (p. 511) gives rubric 10 'statut de la syllabe pénultième' = 'accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur)': fixed penultimate prominence by length, tone system separate. This is the best first-hand statement read (no catalog source to supersede). Beyond the target list I found and read Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 (BLS 18, open PDF, scanned), which states for Mijikenda incl. Chidigo that 'the penultimate syllable is metrically prominent' (p. 29). Not obtainable by automated download: Nicolle's SIL grammar of Digo (2013; rev. 2023) -- SIL records say 'Not Available Online', print only; its phonology chapter is the highest-priority acquisition for a direct stress statement. Kisseberth 1984 'Digo tonology' is paywalled at De Gruyter (doi 10.1515/9783110864465.105); Kisseberth & Wood 1980 / Kisseberth 1981 (SLS) sit on IDEALS, which could not be reached by automated download throughout; Nurse & Hinnebusch 1993 is print only.org was 'Temporarily Offline'; what I did read came via direct automated download to ddl.cnrs.fr, journals.linguisticsociety.org, sil.org, theses.fr, Crossref and the local Glottolog 5.1 sources.bib.

new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (38 pp., text). p. 2 carries running head 142 and reads verbatim: "The penultimate vowel, it will be observed, is the primary locus of pitch differences (and is also characterized by vowel lengthening, which we have not indicated in our transcriptions)." p. 8 (running head 148) reads verbatim: "Second, we assume that there is a rule in Digo that accents the penultimate vowel of the word. In accordance with general practice in autosegmental phonology, this accent will be indicated by a 'star' (*) over the penult vowel. Third, we assume that there is a rule of HIGH TONE DISPLACEMENT in Digo that says: draw an association line between a high tone and the starred (accented) vowel." Only…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Digo is a tone language (privative H tones displaced rightward), and the penultimate vowel of the word is the metrically prominent (accented) position: it carries vowel lengthening and is where the pitch contrast is realized, with the word's rightmost H attracted to it (surfacing as a level H on the penult before a voiced obstruent, otherwise as rising on the penult plus falling on the final). In our terms: fixed penultimate prominence realized as length, within a tonal system; the source never uses the word 'stress'.
new_statements.exceptions: When the consonant before the final vowel is not a voiced obstruent the penult H surfaces as a rising-falling contour over the last two vowels (p. 148); Kisseberth 1981 (p. 74) later proposes that High Tone Displacement targets the ultimate rather than the penultimate vowel, while keeping the penult as the phonetic locus; Philippson 1991 (p. 166) treats the final syllable as extrametrical. Penult lengthening applies 'in penultimate position in the phrase' (p. 151), i.e. it is phrase-final/pre-pausal.
new_statements.domain_note: Verb words pronounced in isolation (K&W 1980 Part I); the accent rule is stated for 'the penultimate vowel of the word', but the length cue is described as phrase-penultimate (p. 151) and Kisseberth 1981 describes the tonal realization 'at the end of an' utterance. Data from one speaker from Tanga, northern Tanzania (1979).
new_statements.identity_note: Kisseberth & Wood 1980 describe the speech of one speaker from Tanga, northern Tanzania (southern/Tanzanian Digo); Nicolle's grammar and the BTL materials describe Northern Digo of Kwale, Kenya. Glottolog lists no dialect languoids under digo1243 in our data, so no separate glottocode is given. Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 treat Chidigo as one of nine Mijikenda varieties sharing penultimate metrical prominence.

new_statements.quote: p. 511: "Digo : 1. : non 2. : oui 3. : langue accentuelle à mélodie H* 4. : 3 [...] 8. : syllabe finale extra-métrique; pieds illimités d'au moins trois mores; le H s'associe à la finale du dernier pied [...] 10. : accent démarcatif (culmination de longueur)" -- p. 483: "c) langues à culmination de longueur, mais non de hauteur, sur la pénultième (langues à prosodèmes distinctifs, mais sans opposition de longueur) : [...] mwani, comorien, pokomo, mijikenda; [...]"
new_statements.translation: p. 511: 'Digo: 1 [realised length contrast]: no; 2 [underlying length contrast]: yes; 3: accentual language with H melody; 4: 3 [prosodic schemes of disyllabic noun stems] ... 8: final syllable extrametrical; unbounded feet of at least three moras; the H links to the last syllable of the last foot ... 10 [status of the penultimate syllable]: demarcative accent (culmination of length)'. p. 483: '(c) languages with a culmination of length, but not of pitch, on the penultimate syllable (languages with distinctive prosodemes but without a length opposition): ... Mwani, Comorian, Pokomo, Mijikenda ...'.
new_statements.citation: Philippson, Gérard. 1991. Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique Orientale: étude comparative typologique et diachronique. Thèse de Doctorat d'Etat, Université Paris V, 542 pp.
new_statements.locator: Annexe, Digo profile, p. 511, rubric 10 (rubric key p. 497: '10. statut de la syllabe pénultième'); corroborated by ch. 6 sec. 3.5.2 p. 483 (type c) and ch. 4 sec. 4.4 pp. 161-176
new_statements.reading: Digo has a fixed, non-contrastive penultimate word prominence realised as lengthening (a 'demarcative accent' by length culmination, not by pitch), alongside a restricted H-tone system in which the lexically marked stem syllable ('accent' in Philippson's metrical sense) anchors a single H that surfaces on the final or, before a voiced obstruent, the penultimate syllable, with the final syllable extrametrical. For catalog purposes: penultimate (fixed) stress/length prominence; tone present. Cassimjee & Kisseberth 1992 p. 29 independently call the Mijikenda (incl. Chidigo) penultimate syllable 'metrically prominent'.
new_statements.found_by: works with stress in the title

sources.note: Digo is analysed as an 'accentual language with H melody' (lexical marks anchor a single H tone; final syllable extrametrical; feet of at least three moras, H linked to the final syllable of the last foot -- pp. 161-176, following Kisseberth 1984 with a metrical reanalysis). Separately from that tonal 'accent', the penultimate syllable carries a demarcative accent realised as a culmination of LENGTH but not of pitch (rubric 10 = status of the penultimate syllable; p. 483 places Mijikenda, hence Digo, in type (c): penultimate length culmination without pitch culmination). sources.note: Digo is tonal (H tones displaced rightward); the penultimate vowel is 'the primary locus of pitch differences' and 'is also characterized by vowel lengthening' (p. 142); 'we assume that there is a rule in Digo that accents the penultimate vowel of the word' and High Tone Displacement links a H to that starred (accented) vowel (p. 148); root vowels are 'pronounced long when in penultimate position in the phrase' (p. 151). The word 'stress' is not used.

sources.quote: p. 29: "In Mijikenda, there is overwhelming evidence that a (pre-penultimate) High tone is attracted to the penultimate syllable of the representation. We believe that this attraction-to-the-penult is actually a case of attraction-to-accent, i.e. we believe that the penultimate syllable is metrically prominent and that a High tone located earlier in the word is attracted to this prominence (rather than to the penultimate syllable as such)." p. 30: "the High tone appears on the penult syllable of the word (in Chidigo, the fact that the penultimate syllable is the target is obscured, since in the examples above the High tone surfaces as a rising-falling pattern over the last two syllables"
sources.locator: sec. 3 'Mijikenda', p. 29 (and p. 30 for the Chidigo surface pattern)
sources.note: p. 29 (Mijikenda, nine varieties incl. Chidigo): 'we believe that the penultimate syllable is metrically prominent and that a High tone located earlier in the word is attracted to this prominence'; p. 30: in Chidigo the penult H surfaces as a rising-falling sequence over the last two syllables unless the final syllable has a depressor onset.

sources.citation: Kisseberth, Charles W. 1981. Displaced tones in Digo (Part 2). Studies in the Linguistic Sciences 11(1): 73-120.
sources.note: p. 73-74: recalls that K&W assign a 'star' to the penultimate vowel of a word; the author now prefers to say the rightmost H reassociates to the ULTIMATE vowel rather than the penult, and states an inclination toward an accentual analysis (forthcoming 'An Accentual Account of Digo Tonology'). Phonetics: level H on the penult before a voiced obstruent, otherwise rising on the penult + falling on the ultimate, phrase-finally (p. 75).
